Flowserve's Industrial Positioning

The firm said Texas-based equipment maker Flowserve's pumps, valves, and related products place it well to capture reindustrialization spending, including in nuclear power generation. Disruptions in the Middle East that have delayed deliveries could later support new orders for reconstruction and pipeline work. Starboard projected high-single-digit or stronger revenue growth, supported by a record backlog, and operating margins above 22% by 2030 as the start of a longer expansion, Bloomberg said.

In May, Starboard wrote to Flowserve's board urging it to improve operating margins and accelerate revenue growth.

"Flowserve is a great business in a strong industry that has been held back by inconsistent execution. The company trades at a significant discount to peers – even before accounting for Flowserve's substantial opportunity to improve margins and earnings. With improved performance, we believe the value creation potential at Flowserve is considerable," Starboard then wrote.

Riot Platforms' Data-Center Shift

With regard to Riot, Starboard believes approved power projects in Texas, along with a signed lease with Anthropic and longer-term arrangements with Advanced Micro Devices, position the company for the data-center boom, as reported by Bloomberg.

Pricing at the top of the $80 to $85 range would push Anthropic's total offering, which includes a $26 billion private placement, past $96 billion.

Major semiconductor firms, including Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices, have committed to purchasing shares in the private placement at the final IPO price.

The company will list on the Nasdaq under the ticker 'ANT' on Thursday.

Claude developer Anthropic PBC is weighing an initial public offering price between $80 and $85 per share, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday.

The upper limit of that target range would generate as much as $70 billion from the base offering alone, according to people familiar with the internal IPO discussions quoted by Bloomberg. Combined with a separate $26 billion private placement, the total capital raised would exceed $96 billion, without expanding the number of shares available.

However, discussions are still underway and executives have not yet finalized the pricing. A representative for Anthropic did not immediately reply to Stocktwits' request for comment.

Surpassing SpaceX

If finalized at the $85 mark, Anthropic's combined offering would surpass SpaceX's landmark debut, which raised $75 billion in its base offering and $86.2 billion after accounting for overallotment options.

Regulatory filings indicate that Anthropic previously marketed a base offering of 801.4 million shares, alongside 23.6 million shares offered by existing investors, at an initial target range of $70 to $78 per share.

Those filings also reveal that leading chipmakers, including Nvidia Corp.(NVDA) and Advanced Micro Devices Inc.(AMD), have agreed to participate in the $26 billion private placement at the eventual IPO price.

Additionally, assuming an approximate $1.5 trillion valuation, Anthropic (ANT) would command a valuation multiple of nearly 8.5 times projected revenue, aligning its pricing with mega-cap tech giants like Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) and Alphabet Inc. (GOOGL), according to New Street Research analyst Pierre Ferragu.

First Listed Frontier Lab

The debut represents a watershed moment for the technology sector, as Anthropic will become the first "frontier" AI laboratory to trade publicly, beating chief rival OpenAI, which is not expected to pursue a listing until at least 2027.

Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and Morgan Stanley are serving as the lead underwriters for the offering, supported by a syndicate of 20 additional financial institutions. Shares of Anthropic are scheduled to begin trading Thursday on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol 'ANT'.

title: Marvell And Intel Halved: How Long Until They Recover?

Marvell And Intel Halved: How Long Until They Recover?
Trefis Team

Image from Pixabay

Marvell and Intel have both lost more than half their value since June. At Tuesday's close on Nov 17, Marvell stood at $148.74. That is 53.0% below its high close of $316.43 on June 4. Intel closed at $55.17, 60.9% below its June 22 high. Most talk about the chip selloff is a buy-the-dip call or a warning that the AI trade is over. This article asks a narrower question. When a chip stock halves, how often does it get back to its high, and how long does it take?

Mostly they do come back, but the wait has ranged from months to decades. We looked at 20 chip stocks listed today, with daily prices since 1999. They had 57 falls of 50% or more from a high close. In 49 of them, the stock later closed back at or above the old high. The big difference is timing. Falls from highs set in 2002 or later took a median 1.2 years to recover. Falls from the dot-com highs took a median 16.4 years.

Intel is the clearest example. It halved from its August 2000 high and only closed back above it on April 24, 2026. That took 25.5 years. In June it set a new high of $140.94. Since Oct 30 it has been halved again.

This question sits inside the larger AI story we follow every day.

How We Counted A Halving

The test uses closing prices adjusted for stock splits. A fall starts on the first close at least 50% below the highest close so far. It ends when the stock closes at or above that high again. We measure the wait from that first close 50% down. One limit matters. The list holds only companies that are still listed. Chip companies that were bought out or delisted are not in it. We think that makes the true recovery rate for all chip stocks lower than these numbers. Adding dividends barely changes the result. On that basis, 49 of 57 falls still recovered.

Two Very Different Kinds Of Crash

Across all the falls, quick recoveries were rare. Of the halvings at least a year old, 24.0% got back to the high within a year. Of those at least five years old, 47.1% got back within five years. Those totals hide two very different groups.

The dot-com group fell much further. Every one of its 21 falls recovered in the end. But most of them took more than ten years. Micron needed 21.3 years. AMD needed 19.3 years.

Later falls were shallower and shorter. The chip peak of late 2021 is the closest recent test. Eight chip stocks halved from highs set between September 2021 and January 2022. All eight got back to the high, in 1.0 to 3.2 years. Nvidia took 1.0 years and Marvell took 2.4 years.

Most Popular Narrative: 56.8% Undervalued

Against a last close of $24.14, the most followed valuation narrative on Super Micro Computer points to a fair value of $55.85 and frames the stock as heavily discounted relative to that anchor, with the gap explained by how investors are treating AI spending cycles and trust risk today. According to RogueEP, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community who wrote the narrative, the current setup is less about blue sky growth stories and more about what the cash flows look like under tougher assumptions.

SMCI is a good-stock-not-great-company setup: a narrow, cycle-renewed moat and structurally thin margins, but priced at approximately 3.9x our model's FY28E EBITDA with net cash, above-Street revenue momentum and a decaying trust discount. Our framework is appropriately hard-nosed, with an 11.4% WACC which includes a 25 bps FED rate hike, a DCF that embeds a 48% peak-to-trough AI capex bust, and applied multiples at 35-69% discounts to the 10.12x EV/EBITDA and 1.61x EV/REVENUE peer medians. It still produces a $55.85 blended target, 46.6% above our $38.09 reference price.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) stock looks too cheap for its growth outlook. The leading semiconductor foundry has fallen with the wider artificial intelligence (AI) trade. Shares are down roughly 26% since hitting an early-October peak of $487, pulled down by a semiconductor sell-off triggered by leadership turmoil at Nvidia (NVDA) and fresh U.S. export curbs.

On the company's third-quarter earnings call in October, CEO C.C. Wei said, "demand for our leading-edge technologies continues to be extremely robust." The company's October 2026 revenue also grew 59.7% year-over-year.

While AI spending could disappoint, and China restrictions carry real consequences, TSMC's customers still need more advanced manufacturing capacity than it can supply. At about 15.38x next year's earnings, I think the sell-off offers an attractive entry point. I therefore rate TSM stock a Buy.

AI Fears Have Overshadowed TSMC's Position

AI fears have overshadowed TSMC's position, in my view. Investors are questioning whether hyperscalers will earn adequate returns on enormous infrastructure spending. Nvidia's leadership turmoil has intensified uncertainty around its China business. The announcement from Washington earlier this week adds tougher foundry-customer checks and restrictions targeting China's remote access to advanced AI computing.

Those developments can remove potential orders. Nvidia is a major customer, and a broader spending slowdown would affect TSMC. Its customer diversity doesn't protect it from an industry-wide retrenchment. Rather, it provides exposure across competing chip designs.

Nvidia could lose some accelerator share while AMD (AMD) gains it. Both companies rely on TSMC for advanced manufacturing. Google (GOOGL) and Amazon's (AMZN) custom accelerators provide other routes for AI spending to reach the foundry.

Broadcom's (AVGO) designs are another example. Its latest quarterly filing says TSMC produced roughly 95% of wafers supplied by its contract manufacturers during the first nine months. So changing winners among chip designers needn't mean fewer orders for TSMC. That distinction is central to my thesis. Customers can compete fiercely over AI profits while continuing to buy manufacturing services from the same supplier.

Micron Technology (MU) stock returned 189% over the past twelve months, against 10.3% for the S&P 500. That is even after a 21.3% drop in the past month. You would be buying profits at their peak. Micron's net margin over its latest four fiscal quarters is 63.8%. That is its highest at any quarter end in our data, which start in fiscal 2017. So what could a share bought at today's price still make you over the next three years?

Micron Stock Would Be Worth About A Fifth More

Under this scenario, a Micron share bought today would be worth about 21.2% more three years from now, or about 6.6% a year. The model assumes revenue grows 30% a year, the highest rate it allows. It calculates the net margin at 70% of today's level plus 30% of its average at earlier quarter ends. Investors are also assumed to pay three-quarters of today's P/E. That is the lowest P/E the model allows. It applies because the assumed growth is far slower than Micron's recent pace.

All of that gain comes from Micron's revenue, which more than doubles in the scenario. The lower margin and the lower P/E each pull the value back down. In fiscal 2025, the year before the latest results, the Cloud Memory Business Unit became Micron's largest business, with revenue up 256.6% to $13.5 billion.

Micron Has To Sell More Memory At High Prices

Micron's own outlook points in that direction for now. In its September 30 results release, the company said AI-driven demand positions it for a record fiscal 2027. Management's guide for fiscal Q1 2027 forecasts revenue of $60 billion to $63 billion. That stands above the $54.2 billion reported for fiscal Q4 2026, though it covers a single quarter rather than a yearly pace.

Management said that guide assumes only single-digit growth in the amount of memory shipped from the quarter before. Management expects the market to stay tight through 2028, with start-up costs partly offsetting higher prices and a better product mix. It also expects margins to widen through the rest of fiscal 2027 as prices keep rising, though more slowly.

title: What Sent Intel Stock Lower Since May?
detail:
What Sent Intel Stock Lower Since May?
Trefis Team

NVDA

Explore stocks on Coinbase

Intel (INTC) stock fell 53.4% between May 21 and November 17, 2026, while the S&P 500 slipped 0.9% over the same dates. The shares first climbed to a $140.94 close on June 22. By the October 29 close, they had slid to $92.07, 22% below the May 21 close. The steepest day came next: a 28.6% drop on October 30, the session after Intel's October 29 earnings call. The stock then lost another 16% by the November 17 close. On the October 29 call, management said strong data center momentum was partly offset by weakness in PC chips. So what did the call show about each business?

Intel Expects Its PC Chip Sales To Fall Further

Management reported third-quarter PC chip revenue of $8.1 billion. That was down 9% from the second quarter and below the company's own expectations. Executives blamed higher memory prices and limited IT budgets. They expect PC chip revenue to fall more than 20% from the third quarter to the fourth.

This matters because PC chips were Intel's largest business, delivering $32.2 billion of revenue in fiscal 2025. Management now expects industry-wide PC unit sales to fall about 12% in 2026 and roughly 10% in 2027.

Management reported third-quarter revenue of $16.5 billion and guided the fourth quarter to $15 billion to $16 billion. That guide includes about $300 million of lost sales. An accident in early October led to an extended shutdown at Intel's Israel factory.

Management Does Not Expect Positive Cash Flow In 2027

Management called 2027 an investment year. Gross capital spending is set to rise strongly from the $20 billion Intel is on track to spend in 2026. Management said it does not expect positive cash flow in 2027. Cash flow is already thin. Over the twelve months to September 26, Intel turned $59.9 billion of revenue into $3.77 billion of free cash flow.

Intel also reported a $12.0 billion net loss over those twelve months. Most of that loss came in the June quarter. Intel lost $11.0 billion that quarter even though it earned $1.97 billion of operating income. So the loss came from items below operating income.

The slide also started from a very high valuation. At the end of June, Intel was priced at 12.5 times its sales, higher than at every other quarter end since late 2016. At the November 17 close, buyers still paid 4.8 times sales, more than the 3.2 times for the S&P 500.

Intel's Data Center Sales Are Still Growing

Intel's server chips are still growing fast. Management said data center revenue was $7.3 billion in the third quarter, up nearly 80% from a year earlier. It said demand still meaningfully exceeds what Intel can supply. It guided that business to grow by a mid-teens percentage from the third quarter to the fourth. Almost all of the Israel factory hit falls on 10-nanometer server products.
